cells.tense: You are at the table with the pen, and the numbers are landing even.
cells.act: count it out and read what the numbers show
cells.ask: Take one arrangement you've been holding level by feel — who covers what, who owes what — and count it out on paper this week. Read what the numbers say, then adjust once where they point.
cells.core:
You can look at a lopsided arrangement and see what it actually is. The extra someone's carrying, the share that quietly isn't coming back — none of it gets past you, and you can name it without turning the room cold. That plainness is most of what keeps things fair around you.

What's already working doesn't need much. Keep it that way. This week, take one arrangement you've been leveling by feel and count it out — what each side gives, what each side gets. Read what the numbers show and adjust once, wherever they point. You'll know within minutes. Putting it on paper doesn't make it rigid. It just lets the fairness outlive your attention.
cells.sheetLine: You can say what's lopsided without making it a fight.
cells.verb: seeing what is actually there until nothing is left hidden
cells.place: where fair shares get weighed and adjusted

cells.tense: You will run the audit again before anyone has had a chance to move.
cells.act: catch the first spark before you point it anywhere
cells.ask: When a split is up in the air, hold off. Say the first thing you notice, nothing more, and leave the rest unmeasured overnight.
cells.core:
You can spot where a thing tilts the moment it tilts. Lately that means you're settling it before it's had a chance to move — measuring each share, running the audit again, bracing for the next unfairness before it arrives. The correcting takes longer than the thing it was protecting, and anyone sharing the table can feel themselves being weighed.

Clarity at this pitch isn't seeing more. It's refusing to let anything stay unsettled long enough to look at. So catch the spark instead. When a split comes up, say the first thing you notice and stop there — nothing measured until morning. What's out of proportion won't get worse overnight. You'll still see it. It just won't be you holding the scale.

cells.tense: You saw it clearly once, and you've been standing at that door since.
cells.act: hold the first resource in your hand before investing it
cells.ask: Take one uneven arrangement you're still carrying. Before doing anything about it, set down a single line naming what it is for — then keep that line unchanged seven days.
cells.core:
There's something you can plainly see, and you've done nothing with what you saw. A weight you're still carrying, a share that went out and didn't return — you called it right and then went on as if that settled it. It didn't. Understanding that stops at the glance isn't finished; glancing is one cut, and the next one turns it into something you can hold.

So take the smallest piece. One uneven arrangement. Before you do anything about it — a conversation, a change, a line drawn — set down in one line what that situation is actually for, in your case. Then leave that line alone all week. Read it Saturday. What you're holding isn't a decision yet. It's the first thing you've chosen to keep.
cells.sheetLine: You saw it right and did nothing with it.
cells.verb: seeing what is actually there until nothing is left hidden

cells.tense: You are already adjusting what's uneven, and asked, you'd say it just evened out on its own.
cells.act: receive the thing that is coming instead of bracing for it
cells.ask: As you reach to even something out, wait ten seconds. Take in whatever has entered since your last check — the updated amount, the changed person — then correct it only as it stands now.
cells.core:
You can see a lopsided thing and even it out in the same motion — a shift in who covers what, a quiet extra that goes to whoever needs it, a step back so someone else lands first. Asked about it, you'd say it sorted itself. It didn't. And the clear sight guiding it is accurate, which is exactly why the hand stays invisible, even to you.

When you feel a thing tilt and reach to correct it, pause ten seconds. That's all — ten seconds, and take stock of what's here now, since your last check. The split you remember may not be the split on the table. Then move, if the correction still fits. What's already clear to you is yours. Meeting what arrives puts your name on it.
